01.event: When the sons of Yudan the maidservant were freed, Rav Aha bar Ya'akov allowed them to marry each other's wives.
01.turn: Rava challenged him that Rav Sheshet had prohibited exactly this.
01.outcome: Rav Aha stood by his ruling: Rav Sheshet prohibits and I permit.
01.summary: The sons of a freed maidservant named Yudan wanted to marry each other's former wives, and Rav Aha bar Ya'akov permitted it. Rava confronted him, pointing out that Rav Sheshet had forbidden such marriages. Rav Aha replied bluntly that Rav Sheshet forbids it and he permits it.

02.event: A marriage contract whose scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature were recognized was brought before Rabbi Abbahu, who intended to validate it.
02.turn: Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the mishna requires the scribe to have signed, not merely written it.
02.summary: A marriage contract came before Rabbi Abbahu; people recognized the scribe's handwriting and the signature of one witness, so he was inclined to declare it valid. Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the rule speaks of a scribe who signed, so handwriting alone is not enough. The text does not say what Rabbi Abbahu finally decided.
02.missing: Rabbi Abbahu's final decision on the document.

03.event: Rabbi Yehoshua was asked how the law rules on the rival wife of a daughter and whether to follow Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel.
03.turn: He refused to decide, saying he feared the two great 'mountains' would crush his skull.
03.outcome: Instead he testified that two great Jerusalem families descended from rival wives and produced High Priests.
03.summary: Sages asked Rabbi Yehoshua which school's ruling to follow on the rival wife of a daughter. He declined, asking why they were putting his head between two great mountains, and said he feared for his skull. He offered instead his testimony that two prominent Jerusalem families were descendants of such rival wives and had produced High Priests.

04.event: Visiting his son-in-law Rav Hisda, Rav Aha bar Abba took his granddaughter onto his lap.
04.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might be betrothed; Rav Aha countered that betrothing a minor violates Rav's ruling, and Rav Hisda retorted that holding a woman violates Shmuel's ruling.
04.outcome: Rav Aha answered that he follows Shmuel's other teaching: everything is permitted for the sake of Heaven.
04.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba came to the house of his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his little granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he wasn't worried she might already be betrothed; Rav Aha shot back that then Rav Hisda would have broken Rav's rule against betrothing a minor daughter. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha was breaking Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman, and Rav Aha closed the exchange by citing another teaching of Shmuel: all is permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.

05.actor: Rav Yehuda, son of Rav Yehezkel
05.event: While Rav Yehezkel taught a mishna to his son Rami, his other son Rav Yehuda told him he was teaching it wrongly.
05.turn: Father and son argued over the version, and Rav Yehuda answered his father's objection.
05.outcome: Shmuel rebuked Rav Yehuda for speaking to his father that way, citing the proper respectful way to correct a parent.
05.summary: Rav Yehezkel was teaching his son Rami a ruling about mixed groups of condemned criminals. His other son, Rav Yehuda, interrupted: 'Father, don't teach it that way,' and proposed a different version; the father raised an objection and the son answered it. Later Shmuel scolded Rav Yehuda, calling him 'big-toothed one,' and told him not to speak to his father like that, since a son should correct a parent only indirectly by quoting the verse.

09.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya as a 'man of thorns', citing a verse that Israel's best are like briers.
09.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse.
09.outcome: He reinterpreted the verse as praise: the best of Israel protect it like a thorn hedge, and will crush the nations.
09.summary: A heretic taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, calling him a man of thorns because a verse says the best of Israel are like a brier. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and told him to read the rest of the verse. He then turned the insult around: just as thorns seal a breach in a fence, the best of Israel protect their people, and they will one day grind the nations underfoot.

11.event: Rabbi Ami publicly declared a man in his neighborhood to be a mamzer.
11.outcome: Rabbi Ami consoled him: by making it known, he had given him life.
11.summary: A man living near Rabbi Ami was publicly declared by him to be a mamzer. The man walked around weeping. Rabbi Ami told him he had actually given him life, since a known mamzer and his line survive.

12.event: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi sent two Sages to examine them.
12.turn: When women told them 'your husbands are coming', they replied 'let them be your husbands'.
12.outcome: Rabbi declared there is no greater refusal than this.
12.summary: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent a pair of Sages to look into the matter. When some women pointed and said, 'Look, your husbands are coming,' the young wives answered, 'Let them be your husbands.' Rabbi ruled that there is no stronger act of refusal than that.

13.event: In Mar Shmuel's days there was a lentil bread which he threw to his dog.
13.turn: Even the dog would not eat it.
13.summary: In the days of Mar Shmuel there was a loaf of lentil bread. Shmuel threw it to his dog, and the dog refused to eat it. It is cited only as evidence about whether such bread is edible.
13.missing: Any further development; the incident is only a brief cited anecdote.

14.event: A mourning woman removed her husband's body from his grave.
14.summary: The text alludes to a well-known incident in which a woman, while mourning, took her husband out of his grave. It is mentioned only as proof that temptation strikes even in mourning; the Hebrew does not tell the story itself.
14.missing: The actual story (her liaison with the guard and why she disinterred her husband) is only supplied by the translator's gloss, not by the text.

16.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify about a matter, and Rav Ashi at first said he did not remember even after Rav Kahana prompted him.
16.turn: Rav Ashi later remembered and testified, but saw Rav Kahana hesitate, fearing he had influenced the testimony.
16.outcome: Rav Ashi assured him he had not relied on his prompting but had worked to remember it himself.
16.summary: Rav Ashi knew some testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. Asked if he remembered it, he said no, and even when Rav Kahana described what happened, Rav Ashi said he did not know. Eventually Rav Ashi remembered and testified, and when he saw Rav Kahana hesitating, he told him: 'Do you think I am relying on you? I made the effort and remembered it myself.'

17.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man from Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract, and hearing her accent he ruled by Mehoza's custom.
17.turn: They told him she was marrying into Neharde'a.
17.outcome: He reversed himself and ruled by Neharde'a's custom, following Shmuel.
17.summary: A woman from Mehoza, married to a man from Neharde'a, came with her family before Rav Nahman. Hearing her Mehoza accent, he said that Babylonia follows Rav's ruling. They pointed out that she was marrying into Neharde'a, and he answered that in that case Neharde'a follows Shmuel.

18.event: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son's match with the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to greet him.
18.turn: At the door, Yehuda bar Mareimar took his leave and seemed reluctant to enter, so Rav Pappa asked what was on his mind, suggesting a teaching of Shmuel about not taking part in transferring inheritance.
18.summary: Rav Pappa arranged a marriage for his son into the family of Abba of Sura and went to supervise the writing of the bride's marriage contract. Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to honor him but turned to leave at the doorway; Rav Pappa invited him in, saw he was unwilling, and asked whether it was because of Shmuel's warning against helping divert an inheritance. The resolution is not in the text shown.
18.missing: How the exchange ended (Yehuda bar Mareimar's answer and whether he entered).

19.actor: a certain man and his heirs
19.event: A man instructed in his will that a dowry be given to his daughter.
19.turn: The cost of a dowry dropped, leaving a difference.
19.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the savings go to the sons.
19.summary: A man left instructions that his daughter be given a dowry. By the time it was provided, dowry goods had become cheaper. Rav Idi bar Avin ruled that the leftover money belongs to the sons, not the daughter. It is a legal case reported mainly for its ruling.

20.event: In a shepherds' village an alleyway ending in a backyard came before Rav Yehuda.
20.outcome: He required nothing to permit carrying there.
20.summary: Rav Yosef recalled that in a shepherds' village there was an alleyway that ended in a backyard, and the question came before Rav Yehuda. He ruled that nothing more was needed to allow carrying there. The incident is cited only as a precedent within a legal argument.
